items.originalTitle: Michael Nielsen took down his book on neural nets
items.summary:
Michael Nielsen has taken down his book on neural networks and deep learning, expressing concern over the rapid advancement of AI systems by frontier labs and the insufficient time humanity has to address associated risks. He believes these developments pose significant catastrophic risks and that continuing to educate people in this area could contribute to the problem.

Nielsen outlines his view that the fundamental threat is not just loss of control to AI but the emergence of easily developed, catastrophic technologies enabled by advanced AI, which outpace social and institutional defenses. He argues that addressing AI safety requires broader societal solutions beyond technical alignment of individual systems, emphasizing the need for global safety measures to manage the destructive potential latent in nature.

items.title: Google introduces DeepCrossAttention to improve transformer residual connections, achieving comparable model quality up to three times faster with minimal parameter increase [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Google's DeepCrossAttention achieves comparable model quality up to 3x faster
items.summary:
Google Research has developed DeepCrossAttention (DCA), a new transformer architecture that enhances residual connections by dynamically combining outputs from previous layers using learnable weights and depth-wise cross-attention. This approach addresses the information dilution problem in traditional residual connections, enabling models to train up to three times faster while maintaining or improving quality with only a slight increase in parameters.

DCA replaces the standard point-wise summation in residual connections with dynamic routing that allows each layer to selectively retrieve features from earlier layers on a per-token basis. Experiments on language modeling and image classification benchmarks demonstrated that DCA improves convergence speed, training stability, and final model performance compared to standard transformers and alternative connection methods.

items.summary: A new study shows that advanced AI models like Claude Fable 5.2, GPT-6.1 Sol, and Gemini 4 Carbon can determine whether a text was written by a human or AI with a simple zero-shot prompt. These models can also identify the AI lab responsible or, in many cases, the exact human author, achieving high accuracy on datasets including anonymous ICML 2020 reviews and prolific Reddit users. The ability depends on the model's exposure to the author's writing during pretraining and the reasoning effort applied. This capability poses significant challenges to anonymity for individuals with substantial online writing, with limited options for defense.

items.title: China's entertainment industry shifts as AI generates over 90% of new micro dramas in 2026, displacing many live actors [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI micro dramas turn China's entertainment industry on its head
items.summary:
In 2026, more than 90% of China's new micro dramas were produced using AI, including actors, voices, and scenes, leading to significant job losses for traditional actors like Oksana. These AI-generated short dramas, often fantasy or romantic-themed and designed for mobile viewing, have become highly popular, with some series drawing billions of views.

The shift to AI production has drastically reduced costs and manpower, allowing small teams to create content that previously required large crews and sets. Despite the volume of AI micro dramas produced, only a small fraction achieve significant viewership or profitability. The Chinese government supports the development of AI-driven cultural content as part of its broader AI adoption goals, though many former actors have turned to other work amid the industry's transformation.

While AI micro dramas dominate short-form content, some industry insiders believe that live human acting will remain essential for longer-form productions due to AI's limitations in conveying subtle emotions and imperfections.

items.originalTitle: OpenAI claims to have solved a 57-year-old math problem at the heart of AI
items.summary:
OpenAI announced a claimed solution to a longstanding mathematical problem in theoretical computer science related to the exponent of square matrix multiplication, a challenge dating back to 1969. Their preprint presents a lower bound matching their previously reported upper bound of 2.25, potentially defining the mathematical limit for this computation central to AI and numerical libraries.

The company released nine manuscripts applying a new geometric theory of tensors to arithmetic complexity and combinatorics, with independent researchers from LMU Munich confirming similar upper bounds using alternative methods. OpenAI also provided a Lean formalization of their proof, though some aspects remain unformalized. This breakthrough could guide future AI infrastructure development by clarifying performance limits in matrix multiplication algorithms.

items.originalTitle: Building a better Dependabot with AI agents
items.summary:
GitHub is enhancing Dependabot by incorporating AI agents to address limitations in current dependency update tools. The new system, exemplified by the Felix project, automates coherent version bumps across multiple files, reads release notes, applies necessary code migrations, and verifies builds before opening pull requests, aiming to reduce manual maintenance and improve security.

Traditional update bots like Dependabot and Renovate often leave fragmented upgrades and require manual intervention for major version changes, leading to merge conflicts and outdated dependencies. Felix uses AI to group related updates, handle major version migrations automatically, and ensure consistency across toolchains and configuration files, running tests in sandbox environments to verify changes before proposing them.

This approach aims to alleviate "dependency burnout" by reducing the manual effort needed to keep software dependencies current and secure, potentially improving developer productivity and software reliability in environments with frequent updates and security vulnerabilities.

items.title: The Information’s 2026 Gift Guide
items.originalTitle: The Information’s 2026 Gift Guide
items.summary:
In a twisted version of future Christmases, perhaps AIs will carry out all the tasks involved in gift giving. But lucky for us, Andy Jassy still has all the bots blocked! So here once again is The Information’s annual Gift Guide, a project that we pursue with as much consideration and rigor as our everyday reporting. None of these items come via a publicist’s pitch, and none of the suggestions contain affiliate links. These are all things that we genuinely love and can picture wrapping up ourselves. Suffice it to say, there’s nothing artificial about our studious consideration and good taste.

Entertainment

I couldn’t afford most Nintendo 64 games growing up, so I was a frequent presence at the local video game rental store: I distinctly remember taking home the original version of “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time”—and needing to return it jusstttt as I was on the cusp of saving Hyrule, the game’s fictional realm, and beating the big baddie, Ganondorf. This Switch 2 remake of the game has given me a shot at redemption. It’s one of the most critically lauded games of the year—and for good reason. The graphics are dazzling, and I can only describe them as “wet”: Everyone looks magnificently dewy. I also cannot overrecommend the nostalgia dopamine hit from getting to rummage through those treasure chests again.—Justin McCraw, senior software engineer

A couple of weeks ago, the internet was abuzz about an AI-generated trailer that imagined an alt-history in which Nazi Germany and America wage some sort of temporal war. Sure, the clip was cool, but I still have my doubts about whether we’re yet at the point where AI can make a comprehensible feature film. In the meantime, there’s “Fatherland,” a 1992 alt-history bestseller from Robert Harris, the ultra-dependable thriller author. It imagines a 1960s landscape where Nazi Germany triumphed in Europe during World War II, and an aging Hitler clings to power. items.summary:
My comment on The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features — Hacker News.

I had a NYT photographer take my picture at my home earlier this year (for a story about Moltbook, oddly enough). At one point I asked if they could fix things up if I had a stain on my shirt and they said absolutely not - they present photographs as they were taken, with cropping and balancing applied but no edits beyond that.

He did spend a bunch of time trying to find the best possible natural lighting for the shots he wanted.

The photo at the top of https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/technology/moltbook-ai-so... is my laptop, taken in my garden, after hunting around for the best spot that didn't have too much glare on the screen. You can see how dirty my screen is, too!

Photography for a newspaper is photo journalism, and they take it seriously.

(Thankfully I did not have a visible stain on my shirt.)

items.title: How Bankers Are Turning Tech Stock Volatility Into Cash [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Bankers Are Turning Tech Stock Volatility Into Cash
items.summary:
Tech firms spending heavily on AI buildouts have flooded the market with new stock sales this year. And with investments in AI infrastructure soaking up so much investor cash, raising money for other capital-hungry areas of tech like quantum computing and robotics is requiring especially creative dealmaking. 

For companies that are already public but need more cash for ambitious projects, sharp swings in their share prices are making it tough to sell more stock at an attractive price. Bankers say one workaround is turning that volatility into a selling point by bundling shares with warrants, which give investors the right to buy more stock later at a locked-in price. If investors are willing to pay up for a chance at a future payoff, companies can sell stock at a premium rather than the usual discount for new share sales. 

One recent example is quantum computing company IonQ, which raised $2 billion in mid-October at a 15% premium to its prior closing price. In the IonQ deal, investors got stock plus warrants to buy more shares at double the stock’s pre-offering price within the next seven years, an extra way for them to profit if IonQ’s stock soars. IonQ has raised $5 billion in total through three such offerings since July 2025, helping pay for an acquisition spree that expanded its business into chip manufacturing and cybersecurity. The company’s stock has been volatile over that period, falling sharply from an October 2025 high of $82, rebounding to about $70 this May and then tumbling again. The shares currently trade around $21. 

With tech investors particularly skittish right now, there’s more reason for cash-hungry companies to pounce on any opportunities to raise money. That’s also boosting the appeal of at-the-market stock sales, which allow companies to sell shares gradually into the open market, giving them the flexibility to take advantage of rallies. And while less conventional ways of raising equity were once viewed on Wall Street as signs of desperation, bankers say that stigma has faded in recent years as companies have embraced the benefits of having more options for raising cash. 

“Historically, ATMs and some of these more creative financing tools have been a bit of a scarlet letter...it was hard to get a management team or board around them,” said Connor Leahey, managing director at Cohen & Co. Capital Markets. “And now it's totally shifted.”

But getting to the public market in the first place has also become much tougher. Investors have had to sop up a surge in new stock issued by already-public tech giants this year alongside mega listings from SpaceX and last week’s debut by Anthropic, with most of those shares performing poorly after their IPOs. The broader market for tech debuts has all but dried up, and Anthropic’s rapid drop below its offering price doesn’t bode well for other IPO hopefuls. 

That helps explain a comparative burst of activity in mergers with special purpose acquisition companies. Five companies went public via a SPAC merger in October, including two space technology firms and a semiconductor tech company, according to data and analytics company Boardroom Alpha. Four more companies have gone public via SPAC so far this month, including robotics company Agility Robotics and spacecraft developer Quantum Space. 

Public debuts via SPAC boomed in 2020 and 2021 before falling sharply in recent years after a string of poorly performing deals and other market headwinds. But companies and bankers are taking a renewed look at SPACs as an IPO alternative. In a SPAC deal, a cash-poor private tech firm is acquired by a cashed-up public shell of a company. (SPAC stands for special purpose acquisition company).

“SPACs are still alive,” said Steven Halperin, co-head of capital solutions and head of public equity markets at Moelis & Co. “And as the IPO market gets more fickle and transaction sizes become larger and larger, will more companies think about going this route?”

One reason why the SPAC route may be more appealing right now is a proposed regulatory change that could make it easier for newly public companies to raise new equity after their debut. One drawback of SPACs is that they don’t guarantee a big infusion of cash, since investors in the SPAC can typically cash out their shares before the merger closes, which they often do if they don’t like the business getting acquired.

The Securities and Exchange Commission in May proposed easing restrictions on stock sales by newly public companies, including ones that go public via a SPAC. Among other changes, the proposal would eliminate a one-year waiting period for newly public companies to register for fast-tracked stock offerings. That could make it easier for those companies to take advantage of rallies in their share prices, including through ATMs and other deals already gaining traction with their public peers.

But companies and bankers are taking a renewed look at SPACs as an IPO alternative. In a SPAC deal, a cash-poor private tech firm is acquired by a cashed-up public shell of a company. (SPAC stands for special purpose acquisition company).

“SPACs are still alive,” said Steven Halperin, co-head of capital solutions and head of public equity markets at Moelis & Co. “And as the IPO market gets more fickle and transaction sizes become larger and larger, will more companies think about going this route?”

One reason why the SPAC route may be more appealing right now is a proposed regulatory change that could make it easier for newly public companies to raise new equity after their debut. One drawback of SPACs is that they don’t guarantee a big infusion of cash, since investors in the SPAC can typically cash out their shares before the merger closes, which they often do if they don’t like the business getting acquired.

The Securities and Exchange Commission in May proposed easing restrictions on stock sales by newly public companies, including ones that go public via a SPAC. Among other changes, the proposal would eliminate a one-year waiting period for newly public companies to register for fast-tracked stock offerings. That could make it easier for those companies to take advantage of rallies in their share prices, including through ATMs and other deals already gaining traction with their public peers.

items.summary:
Anthropic has built its brand in significant part around AI safety, presenting itself as a cautious foil to OpenAI. But the Claude developer has been losing loyalty lately from some safety advocates who say its rapid technological progress—sure to be aided by the funds raised in its blockbuster initial public offering last week—is increasing the chances that AI will run amok.

While OpenAI has struggled with its own safety issues, it operates more like a normal tech startup, but “Anthropic seems more like a cult devoted to creating the machine gods as soon as possible or whatever, and that seems worse,” said Ronny Fernandez, a longtime AI safety proponent who works at Lightcone Infrastructure, the organization that runs the online AI safety forum LessWrong. 

Criticism of Anthropic has grown louder in recent weeks as the company appears to be using its AI models to automate AI research, only a couple months after CEO Dario Amodei called on AI companies to “pace” the technology’s development.

items.originalTitle: AI Stocks’ Big Worry: a Chip Glut
items.summary:
If anyone needs therapy nowadays, it may be tech investors more than Jensen Huang. Let’s face it: The stock market has been a little manic-depressive lately. On Tuesday, for instance, the Jensen-reinstatement rally reversed itself, sending Nvidia stock down nearly 6%, while Anthropic closed below its IPO price. Neoclouds such as CoreWeave and Nebius both dropped 11%.

That’s perhaps a sign that there are some things more important to the market than the fate of any one man, even our “geniuses,” as President Trump calls Huang. Among those things are supply and demand for computing capacity, and what that means both for heavily indebted neoclouds and growth expectations for chip suppliers. Worries that we could be headed for a glut of chips have percolated on Wall Street for months, without much evidence of such a surplus. But on Tuesday, SemiAnalysis published a report saying “we are starting to see signs of a broader pricing cooldown” in the market for Nvidia’s AI chips, citing price cuts by SpaceX. Uh oh.

items.title: In Private Funding, Like IPOs, Big Companies Dominate [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: In Private Funding, Like IPOs, Big Companies Dominate
items.summary:
Shares of Anthropic fell below its $83 IPO price on Tuesday morning, summing up what has been a tough year for IPOs. While a couple of monster IPOs got done—Anthropic and SpaceX—only a handful of others made it through including offerings from SK Hynix, Cerebras and Lime. And as of Tuesday, all of those were trading below their IPO price. 

That makes it the fifth year in a row when the IPO market has been at least a bit disappointing. A bunch of companies are lined up for next year—including OpenAI—but slumping tech valuations fueled by skepticism about the AI boom clouds prospects for 2027. 

In that context, it’s a decent time to take the pulse of startup dealmaking. One thing is clear: as in the IPO market this year, in the private fundraising market, the biggest companies are dominating.

The top 10 private companies have more than doubled their combined valuation from $1.1 trillion to $2.6 trillion in just one year, Goldman’s top tech banker Jane Dunlevie said on stage last week at Goldman Sachs’ annual private tech conference in Las Vegas. 

She was talking about OpenAI, Anthropic, Databricks, Stripe, Waymo, Revolut, Anduril, Ramp, Cognition and Jeff Bezos's Prometheus. And more than half of those—OpenAI, Databricks, Anduril, Stripe, Ramp and Cognition—are now trying to raise billions more.

There’s still plenty of smaller startups emerging. Goldman managed to play matchmaker for more than 400 investors and 400-plus startups in the gilded corridors at the Encore Wynn Hotel. The mood was still electric, though investors are starting to think: as public market valuations fall, how should we value these private companies? 

One reason why private valuations can stay elevated even as public stocks drop is that venture investors tend to zoom in on growth. Many of these AI businesses’ revenues have taken off, even as they bleed money thanks to expensive AI models they run and the chips they need to buy or rent. 

At a fireside chat at last week’s confab, Winston Weinberg, CEO of legal AI startup Harvey, acknowledged that even with fast revenue growth, its gross margins fell to about negative 55% around June. They improved the figure by about 95% in roughly three months. Weinberg said annualized revenue grew from $190 million at the end of last year and expected to end this year with at least $675 million.

“We’re still early in the build out of AI, which means many of the defining companies of this era are not yet public and many investors are just getting to see the potential of those companies, both on growth and margin.” Goldman’s Jane Dunlevie said in an interview on the sidelines. 

She said each tech era has its own tests with investors: for internet companies, it was a path to profit; for subscription software firms, it was predictable revenue and net revenue retention. 

Meanwhile, attendees at the conference were staying hopeful about next year’s IPO market. Some predicted that older venture-backed startups, such as Vercel, Ramp and Plaid, and even the older vertical software companies with some AI makeover, such as AlphaSense and Clio, will finally go public.

In the two days of investors’ schmoozing over fancy desserts and cocktails, a lineup of popular AI, chip and cybersecurity startups, like Legora, Unconventional AI and Abnormal AI fielded dozens of investors’ meeting requests. Many older software startups were trying to remind investors they still exist. They are not getting too much love, say bankers and investors. 

One barometer of who’s important in Las Vegas this year was whom Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon invited to his private dinner at the fancy restaurant Delilah. In attendance: Legora CEO Max Junestrand and Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao, said people familiar with the dinner.

items.originalTitle: OpenAI Preps ‘Athena’ Data Tool to Make its Agents More Accurate
items.summary:
In its effort to win more business customers, OpenAI this fall launched an agent designed to help firms analyze their data and get answers to internal questions about their business. But at least one customer that has used the agent so far has found it isn’t yet accurate enough for widespread use.

That’s a big problem. But OpenAI isn’t sitting still. Representatives of the ChatGPT creator have told some customers and partners that they are developing a data management platform to help the agent perform better, according to the customer and three other people who spoke to OpenAI in recent weeks.

The data management platform, code-named Athena, has similarities to what is known in the industry as a semantic layer, which companies use to create standardized definitions for business metrics such as revenue and customers, one of the people said. This type of software helps agents understand the difference between gross revenue and net revenue, or active and paying customers, the person added.

One of the biggest reasons agents fail when companies use them with large amounts of complex business data is that they have to work out on their own what the data means and how it fits together, said Jason Strimpel, a managing director at Andersen Consulting who helps large companies use AI. 

“A semantic layer gives the agent that context from the start, often with plain-English descriptions of each item, so the agent has to guess less and [can work] faster and more accurately,” he said.

items.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
items.summary:
I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.

Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.

Coding agents in November 2025

Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.

In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:

Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.

This held up.

Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.

Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant.

The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.

Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.

The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.

Fable class models in June/July

We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.

In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.

After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st.

For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these:

In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.

A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.

Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.

I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.

These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.

3D modeling and game development in September/October

Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.
